Editor's Column

Always Psychoanalyze! Historicism and the Psychoanalysis of Culture & Society

Mark Bracher

Mark Bracher

Mark Bracher  

The Hegemony of Historicism in Cultural Criticism

Many intellectuals who, like those of us involved with APCS, want their work to promote social justice view historicism as an essential weapon in their battle against injustice and oppression. When socially committed critics began two decades ago to speak out against the looming hegemony of what they perceived to be the apolitical and hence conservative positions of structuralist and deconstructive modes of literary and cultural analysis, historicism was the banner under which they united. During the past two decades, such critics, taking advantage of historicist disciplinary and curricular structures that have continued to dominate the humanities, have largely succeeded in displacing their apolitical, formalist opponents, with the result that historicism continues to be hegemonic in literary and cultural studies. Fredric Jameson's slogan “Always historicize!” first uttered at the beginning of the previous decade, now goes without saying in many quarters and goes almost without question in all.

While there has been some questioning of various historicist assumptions and procedures, there has been relatively little inquiry concerning the human consequences, psychological and social, of historicism as such. Forgotten is Hayden White's observation (now thirty years old) that “it is worth askin … why the past ought to be studied at all and what function can be served by a contemplation of things under the aspect of history, [i.e.,] why we ought to study things under the aspect of their past-ness rather than under the aspect of their present-ness” (48). For the past decade at least, the answer to this question has seemed obvious: we need historicism either to provide people (ourselves or others) with a sense of identity or to help them escape the narrow confines of their present identities and become more appreciative of otherness and difference (see Southgate).

To what degree are such claims justified? And how do the processes through which historicism pursues these aims compare with the processes through which the psychoanalysis of culture and society might pursue the same goals? Recently, a number of psychoanalytic critics have begun to question whether historicism's hegemony is justified,1 and if APCS and JPCS are to make progress in formulating social, cultural, and educational strategies for promoting social justice and equality, we need to develop this questioning further, in order that we may have a clear understanding of precisely how various modes and aspects of historical knowledge and inquiry might function as resources for, or as obstacles to, the attainment of this goal. We need sustained and systematic inquiries into questions such as: what are the human benefits, and what are the human costs, of learning histories and of viewing present social and cultural phenomena in relation to the past? And what are the human costs and benefits of alternatives to historicism, such as the psychoanalysis of culture and society? In what follows, I want to pursue this line of inquiry by asking: how do the psychological effects produced by historicism compare with those produced by the psychoanalysis of culture and society being advocated by JPCS and its parent organization? I hope my comments will provoke others to inquire further into the respective resources and the relative efficacies of historicism and psychoanalysis in promoting social change.

Introduction: The Reality of Hate

Jews, during the period of the Third Reich, found themselves invested with images of taboo, defilement, and sin. Reading this process on a group psychological level, the culture-wide phobia against touching Jewish flesh coalesced as a new historically constructed taboo, the theme of defilement and abjection taking on a powerful medical and affective valence, enhancing older and more traditionally rooted anti-semitic stereotypes.

A new language of public morality and historical explanation emerged between 1935 and 1942. The taboos on touching Jewish flesh, on having sexual relations with Jews, institutionalized in the 1935 Nuremberg Blood and Marriage Act, reinforced boundaries between good and bad, inside (good, Aryan, white), and outside (bad, dark, Jewish, gypsy). The fear of defilement by the bad generated increased vigilance and became essential to guaranteeing the Kultur-group's sense of its own health and purity. Or, as Julia Kristeva puts it: “It is as if the skin [in this case, the Nazi belief in the cleanliness and inherent superiority of Aryan genes, ‘skin’ understood here as the culture's ideological tunic], a fragile container, no longer guaranteed integrity of one's “own pure and clean self” [that is, one's own and clean blood]” (53). Therefore, from a group psychological perspective, more aggressive actions had to be taken to protect the culture's boundaries from attack and threat, actions whose objective lay in walling or sealing off potential contaminants to the culture's moral and physical body.

In a paranoid situation of perceived threat, the individual—and this is also true for the group—may, in Thomas Ogden's words, experience “his surface (which in a sense is all there is of him) as a hard crust or armor that protects him against unspeakable dangers.” If the fear is unnameable, it will soon enough acquire names; it may even come to be represented by a set of ideological injunctions that various groups in the culture perceive to be true and binding.

The four preceding papers were presented under the rubric of “Psychoanalytic Perspectives on the Social Consciousness of Hatred” at the 1996 APCS conference. Two of the papers (those by Alford and Glass) fall neatly into this category; two of them (those by Burack and Flax) can be interpreted from this perspective but are centered on rather different issues. For reasons that will become apparent as we proceed, I will begin with the latter.

Burack and Flax are both concerned with issues of race and gender, and both find value in postmodern strategies of interpretation. Beyond that, they have differing aims. Burack interrogates psychoanalysis from the perspectives of gay and lesbian sexualities as well as race; Flax analyzes the play of power in the second Judiciary Committee hearings on the Clarence Thomas Supreme Court nomination.

Burack situates herself between psychoanalysis, on the one hand, and the racial and sexual issues it has largely ignored or marginalized, on the other. She attempts to play the difficult role of mediator. She wishes to encourage the psychoanalytic community to take seriously the play of exclusionary power and knowledge in its own disciplinary practices; and she wishes to encourage gays, lesbians, and those who have been assigned the role of racial (racialized) Other to bend psychoanalysis to their own purposes. She believes that, epistemologically, postmodernism is helpful because it “faciliates the challenge to psychoanalysis without establishing new forms of sexual rectitude, authenticity, and discipline,” although she acknowledges that postmodernism is not the “only route by which to criticize the virtual absence of understanding of power relations in psychoanalysis.”

Burack draws the following conclusions from her exploration of psychoanalysis, race, and sexual identities: race and sexuality are “ubiquitous in the very construction of psychoanalytic discourse”; racial and sexual meanings are “inexorably linked” to the binary oppositions through which notions of human identity are constructed; and psychoanalytic thought “participates in, and helps to construct, the kinds of defensive maneuvers that are its self-identified task to identitfy and bring into consciousness.” She also notes that the analysis of racial meanings can occlude the analysis of sexual ones, and that the analysis of sexual meanings can likewise occlude the analysis of racial ones. Hence the importance of including both sets of issues in the interpretation and reconstruction of psychoanalytic theory and practice.

Over the last twenty years, the scope of the phenomenon of incest has grown dramatically among the families of Quebec. Its public denunciation by the media and by courts of law has made it a burning question for our society. But how can we talk about incest without questioning the soil in which it grows, the family? Our newspapers, as sensitive barometers of the public climate, are the privileged tools we turn to in our quest to locate dominant social rumors. In 1994, just as the International Year of the Family was beginning, I decided to cut out at random newspaper articles dealing with incest or parricide, two family dramas that seem to have a parallel development. Here are some extracts of the kinds of stories I collected:

Man of seventy condemned to five years of prison after pleading guilty to numerous counts of incest with his two daughters from 1965 to 1975, and to having had sexual relations with his five granddaughters, from 1989 to 1991…. The accused feels no remorse. (Le Soleil, January 29, 1994, A-1)

Account of orgies at the trial of the “Seven” of St-Paul-du-Nord. A 20-year-old man told the judge that he had been subjected to sexual attacks by his aunts and uncles, in the living room, the kitchen, and the bedroom. “It began with my mother when she rubbed my penis in the bath,” the witness added. The accused parties “would masturbate and penetrate everyone.” (Le Soleil, January 26, 1994, A-2)

Before putting an end to his life under the most unimaginable circumstances, John Vournous, 15, lay down with a sacred image in his hands next to the cadaver of his mother (who he had just killed) and composed a farewell letter to his father, avowing for the last time his undying love and stating that he had never cried more or been filled with so much regret for his irreversible act of destruction…. The adolescent had fraternized with his classmates as usual that day…. His teachers never had any cause to reproach him…. 24 hours after the event, the police were still trying to find some logical explanation for this horrifying story…. (Le Soleil, January 14, 1994, B-8)

Introduction

Most people are unaware of the fact that upon adoption in all states in America except Alaska and Kansas, and most recently Tennessee, a new birth certificate is issued which lists the adoptive parents as the adoptee's birth parents. Adoptees' original birth certificates are then sealed, and access to them by adoptees who are searching for the identity of their birth parents is proscribed by law. The basic rationale upon which these laws rest is that they will set boundaries that will presumably protect and assist adoptive families, and adoptees as well, in their joint task of establishing and developing parent-child bonding in the new adoptive families, and that they will also protect the right to confidentiality of the birth parents so that they can move on with their lives. To accomplish these objectives the door is closed between the adoptee and his birth parents.

There is a growing movement to revoke these laws, which many consider to be unconscionable, and to replace them with new ones. In New Jersey, where adoptees' birth records have been sealed since the passage of Assembly Adoption Bill A-188 in 1940, two identical bills are under consideration, Assembly Bill A-742, and Senate Bill S-287, that would change the current law and authorize adoptees eighteen years of age and older to have access to their original birth certificates. These bills include a provision that birth parents who do not want their identity known would have one year within which to block access. Similar bills are under consideration in other states. Despite strong efforts by the New Jersey Coalition for Openness in Adoption to influence legislators to change current adoption law, many legislators have continued to be opposed to change. Such opposition is not a new phenomenon, and it has been intense. Similar legislation proposed in New Jersey in the past has consistently been defeated.

In this paper I shall advance several arguments in support of the need for change, and answer the objections raised by those who are opposed to change. Although it is argued by proponents of the status quo that current adoption laws are good, and that their goals laudable, there are many problems inherent in them. I shall document that these laws legislate blatant dishonesty, deception, restriction of freedom, and distortion of reality, and cause immeasurable harm to adoptees, birth families, and adoptive families.

Lucie Cantin

Lucie Cantin

Lucie Cantin   Psychologist and psychoanalyst, is Assistant Director of the Psychoanalytic Treatment Center for Adult Psychotics; Vice President of GIFRIC; Clinical Professor in the School of Psychology, Laval University; Editor of Savoir: A Journal of Psychoanalysis and Cultural Analysis; and a member of the European School of Psychoanalysis.

For some years now, issues related to procreation, sexuality, and insanity have been subjected in our so-called “advanced” societies to a treatment which, from the psychoanalyst's point of view, deserves attention. The admittedly rather violent title of this article seems best suited to qualify the issues involved in certain approaches to human problems. Such will at least be the subject of this article, which will mainly examine the new perspectives on paternity and maternity.

Of course, it is not by coincidence that we have chosen the three domains of procreation, sexuality, and insanity. They are all essentially human, insofar as they involve the relation of the subject to the Other, in which the subject is invited to, addressed by, and confronted with the unavoidable necessity of an ethical choice. By defining the relation to the Other as central in this problematics, I want to stress several of its aspects. First, the subject is committed to his or her relation to “jouissance” and speech. Second, the subject is “asked” to act ethically—that is, to make a choice, to take a position that can be justified from no other place but the subject's; such an act is not determined by a logic that would dictate its meaning, but is necessarily without a basis, while requiring that the subject be responsible for it and bear its consequences. And third, this act and this position are always “received” from the Other's place, where the conditions for believability are stated. In his or her relation to the Other, on the most essential issues, the subject is indeed faced with a total absence of guarantee and must ultimately rely on the law and the Other's good faith, both when s/he is in the position of the subject and when s/he is for the other the place that is being addressed.

It is precisely this hole, which Willy Apollon calls a “default of knowledge” (défaut de savoir), that will be masked by the development of a certain type of argumentation. Indeed, in these essentially human domains, our North American societies promote discourses which, on the strength of the scientific basis that would guarantee their truth, propose some biological arguments and facts of nature as both cause and justification for human behavior, thereby offering a biological and real basis that pretends to replace the conditions of believability in the relation of the subject to the Other. These discourses are, to say the least, seductive as they bypass castration, since on one hand they legitimize for the subject the non-necessity of going through the Other's desire, while on the other hand they repress the still ethical dimension of his act, whatever it is. For this refusal of castration also constitutes a choice on the part of the subject in his relation to the Other.

Over the last decade, the various fields subsumed under the rubric of “cultural studies” have centered increasingly on narrative representations of otherness and on how those representations might affect attitudes toward “others” on a psychological and a cultural level. Yet few books have explored the cultural functions of literature as a specifically aesthetic practice as subtly and suggestively as Gabriele Schwab's The Mirror and the Killer-Queen: Otherness in Literary Language. The first of two projected volumes, The Mirror and the Killer-Queen is chiefly concerned with three kinds of literary alterity: figurations of women as other, figurations of otherness along gender boundaries, and the otherness of literary language itself vis à vis other discourses. In Schwab's intriguing hypothesis, encounters with otherness in literature effect a powerful and salutary intervention in our relations with otherness in the extraliterary world. The first chapter provides a brief yet useful and wide-ranging survey of theories—psychoanalytic, hermeneutic, cultural, and French feminist, among others— that treat reading as an encounter with alterity. Drawing on this bricolage of approaches, Schwab proceeds to articulate her own psychoanalytic “ethnography of reading” based on theories of “cultural contact” and “transference.” The remainder of the book comprises six essays on the following texts: Carroll's Alice in Wonderland, Joyce's Finnegan's Wake, John Cage's Roaratorio, Hawthorne's The Scarlet Letter, Faulkner's As I Lay Dying, Djuna Barnes's Nightwood, and Marguerite Duras's The Malady of Death.

According to Schwab, literary texts facilitate “cultural contact” in two registers: intercultural and intracultural. Reading Shakespeare is an instance of intercultural contact, in Schwab's view, for it entails our encountering the historical otherness of Elizabethan language and culture. In the process, we are compelled to seek for something within that otherness that we can respond to and that we can assimilate into our own cultural identities. However, invoking Gregory Bateson's anthropological theory, Schwab observes that cultural contact occurs not only between different cultures, but also encompasses those processes whereby subjects are socialized into their own environments. Literary texts are an important mode of contact in this second, intracultural sense, for literature “engages language as the most basic medium of acculturation” (x). The Mirror is most interesting when it indicates how literature—especially the “experimental” texts of the last century or so—not only reinforces those acculturative processes that shape our attitudes toward otherness, but also subverts them, affording what Schwab calls a “countersocialization” (46). Texts that stubbornly refuse to yield up a coherent narrative or straightforward “meaning” are similar to interactions with human others, insofar as they compel us to move outside habitual modes of thought and communication. Elaborating on her work in Subjects Without Selves, Schwab argues that “[e]xperimental texts require a thinking in open rather than in closed systems which, in turn, tends to increase sensitivity and tolerance for otherness and to decrease cultural paranoia” (44). In her view, such “virtual encounters” with alterity are “a privileged medium for training negotiations across boundaries that demarcate otherness” (45).

The Subversive Value of Symbolic Castration: The Case of Desdemona

Judith Feher-Gurewich

Judith Feher-Gurewich

Judith Feher-Gurewich   Director of the Lacan Seminar at the Center for Literary and Cultural Studies at Harvard Unversity. She is a member of Espace Analytique and of the Association de Formation Psychanalytique et de Recherches Freudiennes of Paris, and an affiliated member of Boston Psychoanalytic Society and Institute. She is also a practicing psychoanalyst in Cambridge, MA, and Director of the series Lacanian Clinical Field at Jason Aronson Publisher.

Freud's view of feminine development has caused much turbulence in the human sciences in general and in feminist theory in particular. The appeal of Lacanian theory for feminists, which lies in its having pulled Freud's ideas away from biological determinism, has even further obscured the insights of the inventor of psychoanalysis. It is generally assumed that Lacan has moved beyond Freud, especially where the question of sexual difference and its relation to the symbolic order are concerned. However, such a “move” has only displaced the patriarchal bias that has been attributed to psychoanalysis. Today it is only when turned against itself that Lacan's reading of Freud serves a function in feminist theory. His concept of symbolic castration is now considered to be the ultimate form of alienation for women, since it condemns them to accept the law of sexual difference and its demeaning social consequences. Hence, in the feminist critical appropriation of Lacan's ideas, Freud incarnates an evil that Lacan has somewhat deceptively perpetuated.

In reaction to this view, I would argue that a reading of the feminine oedipal complex—a reading in which Freud interprets Lacan rather than the reverse—may reveal that feminine castration, far from submitting women to the demands of phallocracy, is on the contrary the condition of its subversion. I must add, however, that this somewhat unusual argument came to me not through my readings of Freud or Lacan, but through my encounter with Shakespeare's character Desdemona. Othello's beloved wife appears to me to be a prime example of a woman who died for having succeeded where Freud suspected she couldn't and where Lacan never really bothered to go and look.

Before we examine Desdemona's psychic success in detail, let's briefly summarize Freud's and Lacan's respective views on the fate of women's oedipal complex. According to Freud, boys and girls relate differently to the oedipal situation; while the prohibition of incest literally forces the boy to replace his erotic bond to his mother with the implacable demands of the superego, the girl enters the oedipal arena with little intention of leaving it. “She enters the oedipal situation as though into a haven or refuge and therefore stays in it for an indeterminate length of time.” Freud adds: “In these circumstances the formation of the super-ego must suffer; it cannot attain the strength and independence which gives it its cultural significance, and feminists are not pleased when we point out to them the effects of this factor upon the average feminine character” (vol. 33: 129). The average feminine character therefore never completely abandons its attachment to its incestuous objects. In the best of cases the woman transmutes her penis envy into a wish for a child—the father's child, of course, as far as the unconscious fantasy is concerned—or extends her desire for the penis to a man who supposedly possesses what she lacks. Freud is careful, however, to add that such a man more often than not occupies the place of the one who initially deprived the daughter of what she most wanted, namely her mother. In other words, one way or another a woman remains dependent on her penis envy. But it's important to note that Freud's rationale is based on what he perceived to be the psychical consequences of the anatomical difference between the sexes. It is on this very point, I would argue, that Freud accepts his responsibility and Lacan does not.

The Sublime Object of Liminality: A Critique of Homi Bhabha

Robert Resch

Robert Resch

Robert Resch   Teaches European intellectual history at Texas A&M University. He is the author of Althusser and the Renewal of Marxist Social Theory and articles on postmodernism, Marxist social theory, and George Orwell. He is currently working on a survey of Lacanian social theory.

In his influential collection of essays, The Location of Culture, Homi Bhabha seeks carefully to preempt any criticism of the self-professed radicalism of his cultural politics from what he views as the old anti-Imperialist, Marxist Left. In “The Commitment to Theory” he disarmingly acknowledges that “in the language of political economy,” it is “legitimate” to represent relations of exploitation and domination in terms of First and Third worlds, and to affirm the existence of “vicious circuits of surplus value linking First world capital and Third world labor” (20). Furthermore, he admits that Western critical theory has often functioned as “ideological Eurocentricity” and served “to contain the effects of difference” (31) in order to establish and maintain the hegemony of the First over the Third worlds.

But Bhabha also rejects the notion of a necessary collusion between Western theory and the hegemony of the West as a power bloc. He believes that Postmodernism in general, and Derridean deconstruction in particular, are central to progressive politics in the Postcolonial era, and that it is essential for Progressives to abandon outmoded, presumably Marxist and Modernist Anticolonialisms which associated knowledge with truth and progress, and political practice with knowledge. It is a “sign of political maturity,” Bhabha insists, to move beyond the “division between theory and radicalism” (21). We must move beyond the politics of binary oppositions by which liberation becomes a “totalizing, Utopian vision of Being and History seeking to transcend the contradictions and ambivalences constituting the very structure of human subjectivity and cultural representation” (19). The language of critique must give up the idea of truth altogether: “My work does not contain the truth, the ‘truth’ is always marked and informed by the ambivalence of the process of emergence” (22). Influenced by theorists such as Ernesto Laclau and Chantal Mouffe (1985), who assert the independence of ideology from economic determination, Bhabha calls for a politics of “negotiation,” not “negation,” of oppositional and antagonistic elements. Because traditional “political referents and priorities—the people, the community, class struggle, anti-racism, gender differences—are not there in some primordial, naturalistic sense” (26), critical theory can be effective only when it abandons “the symptomatic reading” whereby “the nervous tics on the surface of ideology reveal the real materialist contradiction” beneath (25). Rejecting “essentialism,” Bhabha argues that critical theory must become a “negotiation of contradictory and antagonistic instances that opens up hybrid sites and objectives of struggle” (25).

Obsessional and Hysterical Modes of National Identity1

Harold Baker

Harold Baker

Harold Baker   Independent scholar located in Irvine, California. His ongoing research projects include landscape and culture, national identity, and computers in humanistic culture.

… puisque qu'est-ce qu'une chose? sinon ce qui dure, identique, un certain temps.

—J. Lacan (Séminaire XI 40)

The possibility of a psychoanalytic understanding of national identity arises with Lacan's reconceptualization of Freudian theory, and its necessity derives from the tragic impasse of current history. National identity is a defining problem of our times, and its specificity as a problem corresponds to an essential feature of the psychoanalytic situation: a blockage in the deep structure of interlocution, an instability of intersubjective exchange. Lacanian psychoanalysis clearly frames the relationship of subject and other, bringing out the dialectical character of neuroses affecting that relationship; applied to national identity, it frees us from the quixotic attempt to impose “reason” on the national, allowing us rather to see such reason as itself a mode of neurosis aggravating by its action a fundamental conflict or contradiction which it is powerless to resolve. National identity at present appears as a limit to the hegemony of the social/humanistic ratio. In Lacanian terms, national identity becomes real as a consequence of its suppression in the Symbolic, or rather such suppression produces a monstrous Real, which takes the horrific contemporary forms of interethnic violence, repression, displacement, and genocide.

The principal contention of this essay is that national identity has a characteristic semiotic structure deriving from its material and historical premises, and that this structure produces a dialectical alternation in the political reactions which national identity provokes. These dialectically articulated modes of national identity are called obsessional and hysterical, borrowing the schema of neurotic types as it is featured in Lacanian psychoanalysis. The terms obsessional and hysterical are used advisedly, with reference mainly to the semiotic mechanisms which they represent; yet their psychoanalytic meaning is also in play, presenting the political as specifically a realm of neurosis, that is, of primary manipulations and filterings of reality which can only with great labor and difficulty be brought to awareness. Part of the task to be accomplished, then, is to determine the precise kind and degree of reality which can be ascribed to national identity, that which makes it a traumatic “kernel.” The reality of national identity, it will be seen, cannot be derived from any combination of its apparent constituents, but rather illustrates the process by which “material” and “psychical” or “linguistic” realities are taken up into a peculiar topology which ultimately belongs neither to the one nor to the other.

Heaven's Gate and the Postmodern Death Drive

Robert Samuels

Robert Samuels

Robert Samuels   Assistant Professor of English at The George Washington University and Associate Director of APCS. He is the author of Between Philosophy and Psychoanalysis: Lacan's Reconstruction of Freud and Hitchcock's Bi-Textuality: Lacan, Feminisisms, and Queer Theory.

We can interpret the mass suicide of the Heaven's Gate group as a prototypical example of the role played by the symbolic death drive in our current postmodern culture. The members of this group who took their own lives were dominated by a form of discourse that replaced real bodies with symbolic modes of representation. I will posit that their real death was only an extension of their subjective submission to the symbolic order of language and law. By castrating themselves and taking on an androgynous appearance, these subjects displayed a belief that their natural bodies and sexualities could be lost and shed like an un-needed skin or container. What replaced these lost bodies was a postmodern belief system comprised of science fiction, cyber space, and a New Age millennium pseudo-scientific religion.

In order to explain the connections among these symbolic systems and acts of self-destruction, we can employ Freud's theory of the death drive. This concept helps us to understand why and how postmodern subjects desire to replace real sexuality and bodily experiences with virtual symbolic discourses. In Beyond the Pleasure Principle, Freud develops his concept of the death drive in order to account for a series of self-destructive behaviors. In children's games, war neuroses, and anxiety dreams, Freud locates the same desire to repeat a painful experience that goes against the pleasure principle's goal of reducing all forms of tension and excitement. For example, he asks himself why a child who just had a painful experience at the doctor's office will go home and play doctor with another child. If this subject were really dominated by the pleasure principle, he or she would avoid repeating this painful experience. Freud's first hypothesis is that people gain a sense of control and mastery by repeating something in a game and by moving from a position of passivity to one of activity. Thus, the child who passively experiences the painful visit to the doctor is now actively playing out this experience on a fictional level.

In Part I of Three Essays on the Theory of Sexuality, Freud writes concerning perversion that, in most cases “the pathological character in a perversion is found to lie not in the content of the new sexual aim but in its relation to the normal” (161). This is one of Freud's main points in the Three Essays, that “normal” and “perverse” are terms defined in relation to each other: normal just means that which is not perverse, and perverse just means that which is not normal. If the content of one of these terms were to change, then, since it is the relation between them which is the constant, the content of the other would have to change too.

Shelly Skinner   Student in English at Syracuse University, where she is working on a dissertation about Victorian sexualities and social spaces.

To follow the metaphoricity of Diana Fuss' Identification Papers, this book is about traveling with the documentation to prove who you are when the border patrol glares at you and asks: “Where are you going, and how long do you intend to stay?” Even when you feel most certain about your destination, the risk is always that you might get lost or detained. Identification Papers is about the subject's route through identification toward identity, and what gets taken in along the way. As Fuss writes, “identification is the detour through the other that defines a self,” a detour that “follows no predetermined path, nor does it travel outside history and culture” (2-3).

The central contention of Identification Papers is that identification is the subject's cannibalistic, infectious, and failing attempt to recover a lost object—or, as in Lacanian psychoanalysis, to overcome lack which cannot be overcome—through an incorporation, assimilation, and colonization of the other. That is, “internal to the work of identification” is a metaphoric exchange and displacement, “the substitution of one for the other,” or self for other (5). Yet, because identifications are unpredictable and surprising, identity is always at risk of being disrupted by new identifications. An identity may seem to have unity and coherence because some identifications are continually re-enacted, but identifications are always being formed and replaced. As a “detour through the other,” through which the subject arrives at identity, identification is also a metaphoric journey in which the subject constantly loses its way.

183

Tara McGann

Tara McGann   Student in the Columbia University graduate program in English and Comparative Literature.

Andrew Long: Your most recent book, The Indivisible Remainder: An Essay on Schelling and Related Matters, is the second in your series Wo es War, with Verso; it follows The Metastases of Enjoyment. Could you talk about the series Wo es War and about how the Schelling book fits into it?

Slavoj Žižek: The two main parameters of the series are, first, a strict limitation to works which somehow fit this crucial axis: Lacanian psychoanalysis and Marxist theory. The second parameter is to be very dogmatic in terms of Lacanian theory—no opening toward different approaches; for example, pluralist or interdisciplinary approaches were prohibited. The fact is that the strictly dogmatic Lacanian approach combined precisely with a not-post-Marxist approach is what is needed today. Incidentally, there is another book in the series in between the two of mine: The Panopticon Writings [edited by Miran Bozovic], which I think is crucial, because it throws a new light on Bentham's writings. I think that Foucault did not exploit deeply enough what we find in Bentham's panopticon writings. There are incredibly rich reference points for a new theory of power, for a theory of fantasmatic support of power, which are not exploited in Foucault. As the next volume we will have Alan Grosrichard's The Structure of Seraglio, which is important precisely in this moment of renewed anti-Arab, anti-Oriental hatred. The topic of that book is how in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries in the West, oriental despotism was a central notion, but with many ambiguities. What is so interesting is that it wasn't only a negative reference. On the one hand, for the king, the revolutionaries were oriental despots, and for the revolutionaries the king was an oriental despot. But what is more interesting is that he nicely perceived the ambiguity of ideology. It's interesting to see how oriental despotism didn't just work for upper, lower, or middle classes as a way to denigrate the opponent, but also served as a positive reference, as opposed to a Western, confused, decadent situation. For example, in Voltaire and especially in Mozart's The Abduction from the Seraglio, what's interesting is that the West is depicted as low, corrupted, crazy, disorganized. And basically the oriental despot acts as an ideal enlightened monarch.

Andrew Long: In recent lectures, both of you have been emphasizing the space between drive and desire. Could you discuss this and talk about its importance for cultural theory?

Renata Salecl: The reception of Lacan in American cultural theory is based primarily on his earlier writing, where the notion of desire is the most important concept. Of course, the later Lacan moves more from this notion of desire into the domain of drives. A very simple distinction between desire and drive would be that desire is primarily intersubjective. With desire, the notion of the Other is always implied. However, with drive this intersubjectivity somehow gets lost. Drive is what remains when the subject is submitted to the symbolic; it remains as a kind of pressure or force that constantly undermines any point of stability that the subject tries to make in relation to the social symbolic order. So drive is the very link to the notion of jouissance: the boundless enjoyment, the painful enjoyment that very much differs from desire. Desire is never satisfied. Desire means that the subject goes from one object to another and never finds the one that would satisfy him or her. Drive, however, is satisfied. Drive is primarily a circulation around the object, a circulation which with Lacan mostly means that there is a deadly pressure to which the subject is constantly submitted without wanting to be. The whole logic of desire is a kind of liberation from this pressure. When the subject falls into desire, somehow the pressure of drive is less present. So desire for Lacan is in some ways a better thing than drive. Drive involves the satisfaction that the subject gets, but does not want to get. Desire is the endless logic of dissatisfaction which produces as a side effect a satisfaction, but a satisfaction, that is less deadly than the satisfaction of the drive. For Lacan every drive is a death drive and has this kind of deadly element.

For Lacan, the crucial problem of drive also has to do with the termination of analysis. When the subject enters into analysis, his or her crucial question concerns the desire of the Other, and the subject tries to find an answer to the question of his or her own desire. Thus what the subject encounters in analysis is basically two lacks: the lack in him or herself (to which the subject tries to find the answer on the side of the Other) and the lack in the Other. Since the social symbolic order is split, since the Other has lack too, that means that the subject cannot find the answer in the Other. So what happens in analysis is that at the end there are two lacks, lack on the side of the subject and lack on the side of the Other. Is there a solution? What does it mean? How can we deal with these two lacks? One of the explanations of the end of analysis given by Colette Soler is that there is a moment when these two lacks are brought together, and this is the moment when the subject is somehow able to deal with the drive. So what stands in between the two lacks is drive. Drive is the agency that gives the answers to the subject. Nonetheless, the crucial thing is that this drive answers in silence. Which means that the subject does not get the answer.

John Cash's Identity, Ideology and Conflict is, overall, a worthwhile book. Indeed, it can be thought of as two worthwhile books. It is, on the one hand, an analytical intervention into the study of ideology. In this first book, occupying most of Part 1, Cash reviews and analyzes the theories of a disparate galaxy of predecessors—Anthony Giddens, Erich Fromm, Jurgen Habermas, Louis Althusser, to name a few—and assembles from them a subtle and, he claims, more inclusive model of ideology, one “which is at once concerned with the interplay of both social and psychic processes” (25). While some theorists have stressed the economic determinants of ideology, and others its cultural (or simply personal) aspects, Cash sets out a “third approach,” which “appropriates the virtues of both the sociological and psychological approaches whilst overcoming their limitations.” (12). This third approach recognizes that ideology is inevitably freighted with “psychological characteristics.” “[T]he subject cathects the ideological construction to which he or she has been subjected”; this makes him or her an “active party” (71) in ideology's interpellations, not merely their object of address.

On the other hand, Identity, Ideology and Conflict is also an in formed account of Unionist politics in Northern Ireland from 1962 to the present. In this second book, occupying Part 2, the author reviews and comments on positions taken at different junctures in Northern Ireland's struggles by an array of Protestant leaders— includingTerence O'Neill and Ian Paisley—and suggests that they can be accounted for by the more dynamic and nuanced model of ideology he has been developing. As Cash says early on, his study “can be described as an attempt to develop social and political theory with an empirical intent” (8). The material on Unionist politics, then, stands as an elaborated example of Cash's “third approach.”

As I read through Identity, Ideology and Conflict, though, I found it hard to make the transition from the first of these books, on ideology, to the second, on Northern Ireland. Cash has many valuable things to say about the two subjects he treats. What I missed was an applied hermeneutic which would allow for a mutual commentary between them, a movement, that is, from the general discussion Cash offers to the particular history he describes. (Two brief pages on “depth hermeneutics” do not go very far beyond asserting that “all social actors…think and act within a pre-constituted and pre-interpreted domain of symbolic forms” [114].) To the Editor

John C. Sonne's argument on behalf of adoptees' right to the information on their original birth certificates is an important one [“The Psychological Consequences of Ignorance: Adoptees' Right to Know Who their Biological Parents Are,” JPCS 2, 1 (Spring 1997)]. For too many years, the psychological consequences of the erasure of adoptees' biological origins have been ignored, if not compounded by the state's illegalization of such knowledge. Indeed, Sonne's work suggests that in lieu of the adjective “illegitimate,” used for generations to degrade the adopted child, it would be more accurate to say that adopted children have been subjected to a process of legal and cultural delegitimation, in the interest of upholding an idealized nuclear family.

But precisely here one finds a troubling theme in Sonne's essay that requires some careful parsing if we are truly to understand what is at stake in the erasure of the adopted child's biological origins and the resistance on the part of lawmakers and others to legislation that would render to adoptees the right to know those origins. Arguing that the legally sanctioned anonymity provided to birth parents places an unjust and damaging burden upon adopted children, Sonne represents the birth mother as “bad luck for the baby,” narcissistic, and irresponsible. Throughout the essay, the author discusses birth mothers with a degree of misogyny that is as obfuscatory as it is troubling. Pointing to recent cultural artifacts such as the film Losing Isaiah, Drucilla Cornell has recently argued that adoption is represented in public discourse as a war between two women, the birth mother and the adoptive one [“Adoption and Its Progeny,” At the Heart of Freedom Princeton: Princeton UP, forthcoming]. In Sonne's article, another battle emerges: that between the birth mother and her adopted child. That these two sets of conflicts might be the effects of adoption law and thus interrelated seems worthy of consideration; certainly it would be preferable to the negative stereotyping of birth mothers in which this article participates.

Ms. Murphy criticizes my discussion of birth mothers as containing “a degree of misogyny that is as obfuscatory as it is troubling.” Using her own words, not mine, she claims that I have defined birth mothers as “narcissistic and irresponsible.” Again, using her own words, not mine, she also faults me for, as she sees it, setting up a dichotomy between the “ideal of the loving, legitimate mother” and the “voracious beast, tossing the products of her fornication at the doorstep of the nearest orphanage, her self-interest is all that drives her and it drives her to break that holiest of all natural bonds, that of mother love. She is literally a freak of nature, a monster.” Referring to my defense of the adoptee, that he or she should not be seen as a “potential law breaker who is out to harm others,” or “bad luck,” in which I point out that if anyone were to be viewed that way it would be the mothers who oppose their adoptees' right to know, not the adoptees who want to know, Ms. Murphy faults me for setting up what she sees as an unhelpful, polarizing and guilt-inducing dichotomy between birth mothers and adoptees. As it currently stands, the dichotomy is not of my making; it is a fact, and it is more than a dichotomy. It is a one-sided conformation, with most of the power currently held by certain birth mothers—and obviously the men who support them—who oppose adoptees' right to know who their biological parents are. It is not a matter, as Ms. Murphy defines it, of “recirculation of guilt and misogyny.” These opposing mothers, who represent a minority of birth mothers, although literally law abiding, are in essence “breaking the law” of truth. Make no mistake about it, they are adamant and unrelenting, as witness the current opposition to changing the law in Tennessee. Their position has to be equally strongly attacked and discredited, and this point must be driven home to our legislators.

I don't know whether or not Ms. Murphy has attended legislative hearings, met personally with legislators (one of whom was honest enough to admit to me and my colleagues that he had a personal problem in his family network which was causing him to hold back in changing current law even though he saw the harm it was causing), or heard the venomously or icily expressed opposition of some birth mothers, or their defenders, to adoptees' right to know. To the Editor

We write as colleagues from different disciplines—one of us academic, the other clinical—and with different agendas, but we share a commitment to developing Lacanian theory. We are therefore immensely grateful to Mark Bracher for forming APCS, launching JPCS, and initiating debates on a range of important topics. We especially appreciate Bracher's effort, in his most recent Editor's Column (“Always Psychoanalyze! Historicism and the Psychoanalysis of Culture and Society”), to make clear the specificity of the psychoanalytic approach in contradistinction to others. In the spirit of debate this Association fosters, we would like to pursue such distinctions, hoping to enlarge the space of interdisciplinary dialogue where cultural critics and clinicians talk to each other.

We are particularly interested in the crucial distinction between Lacanian clinical process and other kinds of psychoanalytic clinical practice. Bracher is certainly right that some psychoanalytic theorizing serves to secure narcissistic closure, thereby ironically promoting the elaboration of identity-based expressions of subjectivity that contribute to social intolerance. He contrasts this with psychoanalytic clinical process, which provides an opportunity to examine the fantasies that constrain desire —a strategy that might ultimately derail some of the pernicious effects of identity politics. However, we find this comparison of psychoanalytic theory and practice potentially misleading and would like to clarify exactly what's at stake in drawing such comparisons.

Our experience of therapeutic process as theorized and practiced in North American psychoanalytic clinics runs quite contrary to what Bracher leads us to expect. Indeed, to our dismay, much psychoanalytic practice is in the service of—if not specifically devoted to—securing precisely the narcissistic closure that Bracher derides. Although traditionally Lacanians have targeted ego psychology in order to stake their claim, by this point ego psychology, if not passé, is just one of many schools in the post-Freudian and object-relational world of North American psychoanalysis. One need not be a practicing self-psychologist or relational theorist to appreciate the central role played by consolidation of various identifications—sexual, gender, racial, etc.—in most of the clinical process depicted in the trade journals. It seems to us that the very desire for sameness animating historicism's consolidation of identity also virtually dominates the current North American psychoanalytic scene.

Mark Bracher Responds

I thank Tim Dean and Cynthia Dyess for raising several important issues regarding psychoanalysis and historicism. First, there is “the crucial distinction between Lacanian clinical process and other kinds of psychoanalytic clinical practice.” I agree that it is important to distinguish among different kinds of clinical practice, but I do not believe that the most important distinction to be made is necessarily between Lacanian and non-Lacanian practice The crucial distinction, I believe, is that between psychoanalysis as I defined it in my analysis of historicism—that is, a practice that helps people uncover, identify, and own previously rejected parts of themselves—and other, supportive and/or expressive modes of therapy, the basic goal of which is some form of ego-consolidation. Both Lacanian and American analysts practice both kinds of treatment. My own analysis, for example, which was conducted by a training and supervising analyst certified by the American Psychoanalytic Association, involved virtually none of the kind of ego-consolidation that Lacan attributed to ego psychology. Rather than dividing the psychoanalytic world into Lacanian and non-Lacanian, it would be more productive to investigate similarities and differences within as well as between Lacanian and non-Lacanian schools concerning the fundamental aims, the basic strategies, the major techniques, the central processes, and the typical outcomes of psychoanalytic treatment.

It is also important to recognize the value of various supportive and expressive techniques, as, for example, when one is dealing with psychotic patients. Rather than universally disparaging supportive therapy, as some Lacanians do, it is more productive to recognize that for some severely disturbed patients, such work can produce a major improvement in well being, as some Lacanians who work with such patients have themselves recognized. Such a mode of therapy and social intervention should be criticized, however, when it functions to preclude rather than facilitate a person's or group's empowerment.

These words come from two locations of marginalization in US society. Advertising

Yannis Stavrakakis

Yannis Stavrakakis

Yannis Stavrakakis   Member of the Centre for Theoretical Studies in the Humanities and the Social Sciences of the University of Essex, where, under the supervision of Ernesto Laclau, he has completed his doctorate. His main research interests include an exploration of the importance of Lacanian psychoanalysis for political theory (especially the theory of democracy) and socio-political analysis (especially the analysis of Green Ideology). He has published articles in English, German, and Greek and is the APCS International Correspondent for Greece.

Advertising is the part of popular culture which has generated, and still generates, some of the most polemical debates in recent literature. The debate around advertising discourse is usually articulated around three axes: 1) The first axis is structured around the question “‘What’ does advertising do?” Very often it is argued that advertising ignores or distorts the real/natural human needs and puts in their place “false desires.” 2) The second question that dominates the ongoing discussion is “How does advertising work?” Here the “natural” answer is that it does so by simply lying. 3) But why? It is usually argued that the reason is located in advertising's crucial role in maintaining the capitalist system, or the market economy system, if you prefer. It is true, of course, that advertising is essential in stimulating the mass consumption that is needed in the capitalist phase of mass production. Critics of advertising see that as a brainwashing activity that enhances our enslavement to capitalist exploitation while analysts more favorable toward advertising describe it as its central role in the economic reproduction of society.

None can fail to recognize, however, that this organization of the debate does not take into account recent theoretical developments regarding the need/desire and truth/falsity questions. Thus, it cannot really help us in approaching the advertising phenomenon. This is also proved by the fact that the critique of advertising based on the aforementioned assumptions is not effective; that is to say, it is unable to generate a real change in social attitudes toward advertising. Even people who are questioning the status of both market economy and advertising seem unable to organize their desire in an alternative way; thus advertising discourse enjoys a passive legitimation that, in fact, adds to its hegemonic hold.

It is time for a radical reorientation of our approaches to advertising, and Lacanian theory has a lot to offer to such an enterprise. It is not only that Lacan himself referred to advertising—to the slogan “Enjoy Coca-Cola”—while speaking about la sujet de la puissance in his Baltimore lecture in 1966 (Lacan, Replies 51), instituting thus the problematic of enjoyment as the point de capiton of any Lacanian approach to advertising. It is also that psychoanalytic theory constitutes one of the privileged discursive frameworks as far as discussions of need and desire are concerned, not to mention the issue of their truth or falsity— which must have something to do with the fantasmatic dimension of desire and its all too true results.

What can Lacanian theory offer to historiography? This was a question that I began to consider in a recent article in Radical Philosophy (Evans), and which I will now attempt to develop further. In the earlier article I attempted to refute

141

the charge of ahistoricism that is often leveled against Lacanian theory. Basing myself on a reading of some of Lacan's earlier works, I showed that Lacan does not view concepts such as the Oedipus complex or the ego as designating eternal and immutable aspects of the human psyche. On the contrary, a close reading of Lacan's texts shows that these and other features of the psyche are presented by Lacan as phenomena that arise at specific moments in history. By grounding psychic structure in historical processes, Lacan makes it clear that no account of subjectivity, psychoanalytic or otherwise, can claim an eternal, ahistorical validity. Psychoanalytic theory must therefore be read as a description of how subjectivity is constructed at a particular historical moment.

This in itself is not a particularly bold claim. Many others have argued along precisely these lines. The general injunction to be aware of the historical limitations of the categories of thought is a central tenet of all those traditions of critical thinking that trace their descendence, in some way or another, from Marx. What is original about Lacan's remarks on the historicity of psychic structures is that they come from the pen of a psychoanalyst. Whereas Fromm, Marcuse, and others associated with the Frankfurt School were not slow to remark on the historicity of Freud's theories of the mind, most psychoanalysts before Lacan had either completely sidestepped the issue or taken up an implicitly ahistorical stance. Lacan's explicit affirmations of the historical relativity of psychoanalytic theory are therefore unusual, and mark the beginning of a trend in which psychoanalysts themselves begin to question the implicit ahistoricism of previous psychoanalytic theory.

Unlike several academic fields, including women's studies, literary criticism, and philosophical psychology, law and criminology have moved rather slowly to incorporate the rich psychoanalytic insights of Jacques Lacan into their respective pedagogical frames of reference. Two notable figures, however, (David Caudill in law and Dragan Milovanovic in criminology) have gone to great lengths to move the full and reluctant weight of the legal and criminological communities forward. Although certainly not the only Lacanian epigones in their particular academic disciplines (see e.g., Goodrich, Languages of Law, and Arrigo, The Contours of Psychiatric justice), Caudill and Milovanovic represent the next generation of scholars who have considerably advanced the noteworthy project of better understanding the unconscious forces at work in the operation of law and crime.

In their most recent efforts, Caudill and Milovanovic offer collections of previously published essays brought together in single volume form. I generally find this strategy quite appealing, particularly for the degree of accessibility which it gives the reader. Further, this approach makes it possible to examine the development of an author's thinking on a series of issues or on a single matter of import. Finally, the technique is worthwhile when theory is linked with practice such that identifiable controversies (e.g., the law of property, or the prison inmate as jailhouse lawyer) are given new light where fresh interpretations usher forth and novel meaning abounds. Both Caudill and Milovanovic substantially succeed on these fronts and they are to be commended. The respective methods by which they accomplish these goals, however, are decidedly different.

Racialization remains a deep current in the politics of inequality. It has generated severe historical contradictions to the point of crisis for the liberal nation-state, which must reconcile racial logic with the universal aspirations of enlightenment ideology.

(Moallem and Boal 2)1

The Real of Race

The “real” of race is invisible to the naked eye, consisting of microscopic blood factors such as those examined to death in the O. J. Simpson trial. Even these are not sure-fire indicators of race, but statistical correlates. Although, physiologically, races can be said to exist as identifiable breeding populations (or micro-races) with genetic markers, even those markers are mutable with time, geographical mobility, and changes in the breeding pool.2 Persistence of a biological race through time depends on the vagaries of reproductive success. There is no original racial essence. No more than any individual does a “race” have a fixed point of identification.

Yet, psychically and politically, individuals and races alike do have such identifying points: there where they are alienated (“castrated”) in and by a signifier which represents them to other signifiers—signifiers which assign them a place in a symbolic order, and leave out something of their being. Race is, however, a special case of identification. (In English, race has links to words for root, for a sharp hook as well as an erasure. [Oxford Universal Dictionary 1646]). What better example of a Lacanian “point de capiton,” the source of a secondary identification? [Zizek 16 ff.])

The Political Nature of Race

What distinguishes the alienated identification of race as a “quilting point” from that of primary identification by the signifier (to which any and every human subject is submitted) is not that it is more traumatic—it may not be—but that its representation is not essential to the constitution of the universal human subject. One's humanity as a speaking being has no necessary links with any signifier of race. That is not to say racialization has no impact on its subjects. To the contrary, the presence of race among the myriad classificatory schemes devised for keeping social order in unruly, antagonistic, and incomplete symbolic systems has generally involved an intended insult to the core of (and power over) those subjects represented as “racial.” In other words, one can hardly say “race” without racism's going hand in glove (to use another Simpson image). What must be emphasized here, however, is that the very emergence of the signifier “race” is absolutely contingent, dependent upon the desire of a Master to organize subjects in this way.

Editor's Column

Psychoanalysis and Racism

Mark Bracher

Mark Bracher

Mark Bracher  

As the twenty-first century approaches, one of the greatest problems confronting humanity is racism, which afflicts every continent and virtually every country on our planet. The pervasiveness, persistence, and recent resurgence of racism throughout the world make it a phenomenon that anyone concerned with social justice or human welfare must attempt to combat. This is a fortiori the case for an organization like APCS, whose purpose is to use psychoanalysis to promote beneficial social change. The challenge for us is to find ways to use psychoanalysis to help prevent or reduce racism.

Today, many people have dismissed the possibility that psychoanalysis might make a substantial contribution to the reduction of racism. One reason for this skepticism is a general disillusionment with psychoanalysis since the first half of this century, when it seemed to many people to offer a fairly simple, if somewhat arduous, solution for both psychological and social problems. But a more substantive reason is the growing recognition that 1) racism comes in multiple forms, some of which are functions of social structures and institutions and thus appear to have no significant psychological roots, and that 2) even old-fashioned racial prejudice and hatred, which are clearly psychological phenomena, appear to be caused in large part by certain social, political, and economic conditions, intervention in which, it is therefore reasonably assumed, would be a much more effective way to reduce racism than would attempts to alter the subjectivities of large numbers of people.

Socio-Economic Determinants of Racism

Empirical research has demonstrated strong correlations between racism and socio-economic factors. A number of studies have shown, for example, that lower socio-economic status correlates more strongly with racism in South Africa than do those personality traits labeled “authoritarianism,” which some researchers had previously taken to be the major cause of racism and other prejudices.1 Such findings suggest “that social norms rather than individual personality dynamics determine overall levels of prejudice in particular groups” (Brown 33). Other studies have also demonstrated that the social situation is an important cause of racism. Rupert Brown reports a 1951 study in which a six-week human relations workshop resulted in a significant decline in the participants' authoritarianism, and a 1957 study of two groups of American women college students, one housed in a conservative dorm and the other in a dorm with more liberal norms, in which those exposed to the liberal norms showed a decline in authoritarianism, whereas those exposed to the conservative norms did not (31). There is also the empirically established fact that in economically hard times people gravitate toward authoritarian religions, astrology, and other superstitious systems of belief and embrace tougher, more powerful comic strip characters and pet dogs (see Brown 35-6).

In this paper, I will develop a psychoanalytic form of cultural criticism that provides a theoretical framework for the analysis of homophobia, sexism, racism, and ethnocentrism. In order to relate these different modes of oppression to each other, I will define a fundamental cycle of prejudices that is based on the homophobic rejection of same-sex desires, which results in the racist projection of unwanted libidinal impulses onto culturally debased Others. Within this structure, the dominant social order equates homosexual desire with a loss of linguistic control and a break down of the symbolic structure of sexual difference. In order to overcome this sense of symbolic confusion, subjects often force others to submit to a sexist form of symbolic castration.

In order to counter this cycle of prejudice, my work explores the unconscious desires and fears that lead to socially destructive modes of behavior. But while this project stresses the role played by unconscious and subjective aspects of prejudice, it does not concentrate on a purely individual or character-based form of analysis; rather, it emphasizes the way that all unconscious and subjective formations are shaped by larger social forces.1

An example of how subjectivity and prejudices are determined by cultural structures can be found in the fundamental role that homophobia plays in other forms of discrimination. Homophobia is never a purely subjective or personal experience; the rejection of same-sex desire is always tied to a cultural intolerance of a form of sexuality that threatens the foundations of a society based on male-bonding and patriarchal heterosexuality. This means that when particular people or literary characters express their homophobia, they are manifesting an ideology of oppression that has deep structural and cultural roots. Moreover, the general acceptance and internalization of homophobia helps to clear the way for other forms of prejudice that feed off of the rejection and projection of repressed homoerotic desires.

It seems that the field of our relationship to nature is one of the fields in which the Real, in the psychoanalytic sense of the word, is continuously intersecting with our symbolic and imaginary reality. It is in that sense that Žižek, in Tarrying with the Negative, presents the ecological crisis as initiating a period of continuous, everyday encounter with the Real. The unpredictability and severity of natural forces have prompted people, from time immemorial, to attempt to understand and master them through processes of imaginary representation and symbolic integration. This usually entails a symbolization of the Real of nature. The product of this symbolization has frequently been described as a “story” or a “paradigm” about how the world works. We can trace such a story, or many competing stories, in any civilization or cultural ensemble. Primal people often understood planetary forces and natural disastrous events as acts of God. As Mircea Eliade has pointed out, in The Myth of the Eternal Return, for traditional societies, historic profane events such as natural catastrophes, disasters, and misfortunes—that is to say, all encounters with the Real of nature—denote the “void,” the non-existent, the unreal par excellence. Thus, they can only produce unbearable terror. They can be tolerated only if conceived as produced by the breaking of a taboo, by a magical action of an enemy or by the divine will—only if integrated, for example, in a schema of indefinite repetition of archetypes revealed ab origine by Gods and heroes and repeated by men in cosmogonic recreative rituals and myths. As soon as the cause is pinpointed, the suffering of the encounter with the Real of nature becomes tolerable, we have the symbolization of the Real. The suffering now has “a meaning and a cause, hence it can be fitted into a system and explained” (Eliade 98). It is symbolically integrated into a “story” or a “paradigm.”

In modern secular societies, it is usually science that provides the symbolic framework for the symbolization of nature. Ulrich Beck is correct when differentiating the pre-modern encounter with natural disasters that he calls “threats” from modern “risks,” which are the result of human decisions, of decisions that focus on economic advantages within an ideology of industrial progress: “pre-industrial threats, … were ‘strokes of fate’ … attributable to some ‘other’—gods, demons or nature” (Beck 20). This is not possible any more.

At George Washington University, as at many other institutions across the country, creative writing is one option among many other courses in performing arts that students must take to satisfy a general curriculum requirement. These courses are intended, as our catalogue states, to “gain an understanding of the role of the imagination in human life,” and “insight into the interactions between materials, talent, and the imagination (12).” Although students are able to choose courses in music, art, communication, and philosophy, the most popular course chosen, by far, is the creative writing course.

Part of the appeal of the creative writing course may be that it offers students opportunities to explore their identities through writing. In the poetry course I teach, writing definitely becomes an absorbing process of self-examination with ethical as well as psychological dimensions. In my class as in most other classes, student are trained in a wide variety of literary genres from the sonnet to the elegy. Whatever particular poetic form they may imitate in both poetry and fiction, however, students write about themselves. In fact, workshop leaders' exploratory approaches to writing are often similar to and to some extent derived from psychoanalytic techniques—techniques that have become progressively integrated into our culture and into our culture of teaching.

Behn and Twichell's The Practice of Poetry is representative of many currently popular textbooks which argue that the unconscious can be and should be used by aspiring writers. The text offers writing formulas for evoking the unconscious and making use of its contents for the writing of poetry. Students are exhorted by the text to “mine the unconscious.” Sections are headed by titles such as “Ladders to the Dark: The Unconscious as Gold Mine,” “The Self and its Subjects,” and “Accidents, Chance, and the Nonrational.” The book's concern for the unconscious is not mere metaphor and word play. The text attempts to examine seriously psychic processes, and each chapter of the book is thematically tied to the discovery of some layer or dimension of the unconscious.

When we think of Julia Kristeva, we think of a number of far-reaching studies—investigations of language, identity, and culture that combine to form a rich and complex oeuvre. While we may find illuminating any one strand of this theoretical fabric, it is perhaps most edifying to take Kristeva's work as a whole, in order that we may best consider her complex balance of interdisciplinary concerns. In his recent collection of Kristeva's interviews, Ross Mitchell Guberman gives us the opportunity to do just that, in a space that affords us, additionally, a fresh perspective on this theorist's personal and intellectual development. The twenty-three interviews Guberman has selected span twenty years of Kristeva's career, and the seven chapters into which he divides them address the various facets of her life and theory. In some cases, this attempt at comprehensiveness may leave the reader feeling shortchanged: each of the book's major sections contains only three or four interviews, which tend, moreover, to be rather spotty in terms of informative content. Because of this scant treatment of individual subjects, the pieces in the collection are perhaps less enlightening than other, more detailed writings by Kristeva. In this sense I would disagree with Guberman's introductory assertion that those new to Kristeva's work will find the book a useful entrée to her theory. On the other hand, for readers already familiar with Kristeva, the edition provides a thought-provoking overview of her ideas, as well as a rare look at how those ideas have been shaped and honed by biographical events.

These events serve as a springboard for the topics of the book's first section, “Profiles,” in which Kristeva discusses, among other things, the intellectual climate of Europe while she completed her education in France—an experience she counts as crucial to her formation of the sujet-en-procès. This first chapter is somewhat of a grab bag of Kristevan viewpoints, and as such it has less of a focus than the ones that follow it. These later chapters cover areas of “Psychoanalysis,” “Women,” “Culture,” “Theories,” and “Literature,” with the last, “Perspectives,” containing only one interview, which Guberman himself conducted especially for the book. But for the most part, even these more concentrated sections offer an at best sketchy analysis of their nominal topics—a failing we can attribute at least in part, I think, to the idiosyncracies of Kristeva's own discursive style. At times, when her interviewers have proposed a question that touches upon pointed cultural or theoretical matters, Kristeva sees fit to attend to only one element of the question—an element which she may interpret, moreover, in a different sense than has been intended by the questioner. Readers acquainted with Kristeva's work may want to compare these recastings to a rhetorical tendency that shows up in many of her writings, namely to perform—as a way of recapitulating—the polysemy of language about which she theorizes. Nonetheless, in a book that fashions itself as a more straightforward presentation of ideas than one has learned to expect from Kristeva, these occasional digression can be frustrating. Still, inasmuch as they frequently return to her favorite lines of inquiry, they do allow us an illuminating repetition of the subjects most important to Kristeva herself.

In the depths of prostration—she can no longer sleep without waking up from a recurrent nightmare of suffocation—in the depths of a state of anxiety that is driving her nearly to suicide, Rachel seeks the help of an analyst after a series of failed attempts to become pregnant. She has already consulted four specialists, the last of whom urges her to let him attempt a second in vitro insemination. Rachel has no steady companion, and when she speaks of possible fathers for the baby she so desperately wants, she lauds only their physical endowments. These are not men you can count on, but then again none of them really counts in this quest she's on. The person she does trust is the medical specialist.

Her state of prostration is striking, and with it, a more insistent demand, a more insistent longing to experience motherhood, what she refers to as the miracle of birth. She visits one physician after another with the sense of approaching some final deadline. It takes five months of regular meetings for the taut wire of dreams that abruptly shatter her sleep to reveal the circumstances surrounding her own birth: only recently has she found out that she is not the biological daughter of the father who has raised her, but rather the sole fruit of a mother's transgression in a marriage that brought life to five children. It will be the course of analysis that impels her to discover that the family doctor, the very same doctor who helped her mother bring her into the world, is her biological father.

Let us merely point out here that Rachel, in her wish to be a mother, questions maternal desire, her mother's desire as a woman and as a mother, just as she questions in the doctor the desire of a man and a father. At the same time she questions the truth of which her coming into existence is the fruit, a truth that, though silenced, has continued to mark her entire life.

When we witness how Andy (the “real” character in the film) treats his toys in the opening sequence of Toy Story, we get our first hint that toys don't exactly have ideal working conditions. (Later, this idea gets reinforced when we find out that Andy, in contrast to Sid, is a “good” kid.) The toys endure physical abuse at the hands of Andy in this first scene, but this only sets the stage for the real terror that ensues: Andy's birthday party, where he will receive new toys that threaten to make his current ones, in the words of Mr. Potato Head (Don Rickles), “next year's garage-sale fodder for sure.” This threat, which, as the appearance of Buzz Lightyear (Tim Allen) makes clear, is a very real threat, aligns the toys with workers in a global capitalist economy. Like the toys, workers today—and this is precisely what someone like Pat Buchanan speaks to—live in a constant state of fear, fear that transnational corporations will find more attractive replacements for them, either in the form of new technologies or workers in other countries. Toy Story is significant because it speaks to this fear and points beyond it. It is this initial parallel between the situation of Toy Story's toys and contemporary workers, however, that allows us to see the importance of what follows in the film, i.e., the toys coming to class consciousness.

As early as Andy's birthday party, we can see that the toys have already formed an organization to look out for their collective interests. Woody (Tom Hanks) is the leader of this organization, a position he seems to have acquired because he is Andy's favorite toy. When the birthday party begins, Woody calls an emergency meeting of all the toys and directs a reconnaissance operation designed to keep all the toys informed about the gifts—read: potential replacements—that Andy receives at the party. He dispatches the toy army armed with a walkie talkie for communication, and they report back to the other toys. Things seem to have gone pretty well, until Andy opens his last present—a Buzz Lightyear toy. Buzz Lightyear is the newest fad—and more technologically advanced than any of Andy's other toys— and thus quickly wins a place in Andy's heart. The gift of Buzz Lightyear sends all of Andy's toys, who realize the tenuousness of their position, into a collective despair. The organization that they have formed—or which seems to have emerged organically—does a good job of informing them about potential threats (such as Buzz Lightyear), but is powerless to stop them. In this sense, the organization is homologous to an informal chain of company gossip, which manages to keep everyone informed while remaining structurally incapable of action. As far as the toys are concerned, their destiny is out of their hands; the best they can do is gain some foreknowledge about what is to happen, if only in order to brace themselves for the inevitable. This is, of course, one of the most basic levels on which ideology works—especially within the world of late capitalism.
