Trauma: Phenomenology and Theory

In this paper, I focus phenomenologically on the unconscious response to and elaboration of the 1995 Oklahoma City bombing: a trauma, an assault and an insult that violated many peoples' “stimulus barrier” (K. Erikson, Loss; Rangell, Discussion) and symbolic boundary of safety. All terrible events unmask earlier losses, rages, fantasies. But such unmasking does not discount the unconscious significance also of the event itself (Oliner, External).

Trauma—together with the helplessness, the rage, the guilt, the wish to master and to make repair, that is unleashed by trauma—becomes an internal representation, an internal object, which in turn condenses with and receives the additional burden of displacement from other, often far earlier, traumas and the fantasies, feelings, and defenses that arose in their wake. A trauma such as the bombing of the Murrah Federal Building in Oklahoma City can be understood as a public self- and object-representation that condenses with and reawakens the more individual, idiosyncratic, personal ones that have a “perceptual identity” with it (Freud, Dreams).2

This paper contributes to the understanding of the relation between trauma as event, trauma as concept, trauma as experience, trauma as unconscious self- and object-representation, what people bring to trauma, the vicissitudes of the affects following trauma, and how people elaborate disaster narratives after trauma has occurred. Like Volkan (Volkan, Enemies), I argue that losses over symbolic objects such as national territory or corporate leadership in a particular market can feel like real deaths to those who experience them, since they can entail loss of idealized self, loss of idealized self-object fusion, and loss of sense of safety. Similarly, they can be followed by the same “complicated mourning” as the aborted grief of individuals over the loss by death of ambivalently loved ones (Volkan, Cyprus; Linking, Enemies). I wish to avoid the facile ideological split between ascribing all causal meaning to a collective traumatic event (such as atomic bombs, military defeats, concentration camps, punitive treaties, hurricanes, or floods), and equally ascribing all meaning to predisposing unconscious and early family factors (“It doesn't matter what happened.”), and to subsequent elaboration of the event (“What happened?”) (Oliner, External; Berger, Cultural).

On the morning of May 28, 1995, Sinedu Tadesse, a junior at Harvard, stabbed her roommate, Trang-Ho, forty-five times while Trang lay sleeping in her bed in their Harvard dormitory. By the time police arrived, Sinedu had hanged herself in the bathroom. Unlike most killers, the Ethiopian student left a detailed diary of her emotional state in the years leading up to the killing.

Unlike her roommate, Sinedu was not a popular student. She had difficulty finding a roommate and was elated when Trang-Ho agreed to share a suite with her. But they did not get along, in part because Trang's boyfriend frequently slept over, and Trang was looking for another roommate. Sinedu found the humiliation intolerable:

You know what I fear? I fear that shitty cringing feeling that accompanies me…. Should my rooming thing does [sic] not work out in a way that makes me hold my head high & speak of it proudly. (Thernstrom)

If she could have, Sinedu would have inflicted this terrible cringing feeling on her roommate. Only that, it seems, would have made her feel better, and that, she knew, was impossible: “Our situations would never reverse, for me to be the strong & her to be the weak. She'll live on tucked in the warmth & support of her family while I cry alone in the cold.”

It was a situation made worse, or at least more pathetic, by the way so many seemed to confuse them, regarding the roommates as virtually identical non-western exotics. Even at the memorial service, Harvard's minister could not seem to keep victim and executioner straight, referring to both as victims, asking the Lord to forgive them both. “Media accounts made them sound like twins: nice, petite, hardworking foreign-born premed junior biology majors.”

This book features a collection of papers delivered at the Paris “Lacan Seminars in English” in 1990, with members of the École de la Cause freudienne (ECF) giving the majority of the lectures, complemented by contributions made by several scholars from other countries.2 The essays are generally marked by clarity and precision in their explication of Lacanian concepts. The talks given by Miller, Laurent, Soler, Fink, and Quinet, in particular, make this collection by far the best pedagogical tool 1 can find for introducing students to Lacan's Seminar XI.

In contrast to other English publications on Lacan, this book has the additional merit of reading the dynamics of The Four Fundamental Concepts in the context of the institutional struggles carried out by Lacan as he sought to establish his own school of psychoanalysis. One prominent way in which this anthology departs from former Anglo-American Lacanian scholarship is its emphasis on Lacan's difference from, rather than his “return to,” Freud. Miller, Soler, and Fink present very convincing articulations of these differences. Of these, Miller's lecture orients our reading of the entire collection. By outlining Seminar XI against the backdrop of Lacan's “break” from Freud, he enables us to understand anew the concept of the “Name-of-the-Father” and its history (6-7).

The ECF members' critique of the cult of the dead father can assume yet another level of significance for their American addressees. The editors' positioning of the essays by French and American scholars seems to suggest that, in the course of the ECF members' explanation of Lacan's break from Freud, and the Ecole freudienne's break from the International Psychoanalytic Association, a transferential separation between the American scholars and their French predecessors also quietly asserted itself. In the unfolding of the dialectical desire between the subject and its other, between the French “mentors” and their American “disciples,” the subversion of the father in the Lacanian unconscious enacted in this collection by the French Lacanians' marking their own “territory” against preceding psychoanalytic institutions, seems to be then repeated by the Americans vis-à-vis their French “mentors” as the two parties' voices gradually shift in the book.

Elisabeth Young-Bruehl

Elisabeth Young-Bruehl

Elisabeth Young-Bruehl   Professor of Humanities at Haverford College and a candidate at the Philadelphia Association for Psychoanalysis. Her latest book, The Anatomy of Prejudices, was published by Harvard in 1996, and a collection of recent essays, Subject to Biography, will be published by Harvard in 1993.

Introduction

Since the end of the Second World War, social scientific studies of prejudice conducted in this country have come again and again to the same conclusion. Relentlessly, compulsively, they have announced that all prejudices are alike and that all people who are prejudiced are alike, sharing the characteristic that their prejudice against one group entails prejudice against all other groups as well. Intolerance is a general condition: it is a melting pot which so dissolves all differences among prejudiced people and their prejudices that all differences among victim groups dissolve, too. It is not surprising, of course, that this melting pot conclusion has recently been questioned by multiculturalists, who insist that each victim group has its irreducible specificity, its unique victimhood, sometimes its superlative—our suffering is the worst, this prejudice is the least acknowledged, this other one the most ubiquitous or radical. A theoretically inchoate surge of opposition has stressed victim group difference in face of the sameness conclusion. But this opposition frequently dissolves, too, because it does not go beyond victim group differences to focus on prejudiced people or their prejudices; the multiculturalists fall back on the argument that even if all prejudiced people are alike and do hate all out-groups, they can still select out a special target because of something perceived to be in the target.

Psychoanalysis and Marxism, in the post-War collaboration arranged by the Frankfurt School, contributed the first big impetus to the way studies in prejudices have repeated themselves. There is, so the authors of The Authoritarian Personality (1951) argued, a single “prejudiced personality”—a rigid, conventional, puritanical, unintrospective, shallow obsessional type—whose breeding ground is not the class struggle per se but the falsely enlightened bourgeois family under capitalism. It is not antisemites specifically, but rationalistic authoritarian “ethnocentrists” who hate Jews and all other groups who represent nature, primitivity, hedonism. Gordon Allport, in his classic The Nature of Prejudice (1954), popularized this synthetic Freudian-Marxian conclusion by calling all prejudices “ethnocentrism,” in-group hatred of all out-groups. Jean Paul Sartre, too, supported the synthesis in Antisemite an Jew by presenting the antisemite as a petit bourgeois snob who might just as well have displaced his hatred onto Blacks or women—any “pretext,” any scapegoat, any out-group.1

Dragon Milovanovic

Dragon Milovanovic

Dragon Milovanovic   Professor of Criminal Justice at Northeastern Illinois University, Chicago. Among his books are Postmodern Law and Disorder: Psychoanalytic Semiotics, Chaos and Juridic Exegeses; Sociology of Law; Chaos, Criminology and Social Justice; Postmodern Criminology; Constitutive Criminology (with Stuart Henry); and Thinking Critically About Crime (with Brian MacLean). The recent publication of an English translation of Lacan's “A Theoretical Introduction to the Functions of Psychoanalysis in Criminology” is a long awaited and much needed initiative for the development of a Lacanian-informed critical criminology. Lacan's paper is composed of some well established material interspersed with some significant and novel contributions for a critical criminology. One such contribution is that of Renata Salecl, who uses Lacan's work, to postulate three types of crimes: crimes of the ego, crimes of the self, and crimes of the superego. Crimes of the ego are those directed toward simple profit accumulation; those of the self are “pure instinctive crimes which are reactions to some aggression”; and crimes of the superego are those with which psychoanalysis, according to Salecl, has the most interest. These are crimes where a split exists between the ego and the superego causes a subject to try to resolve the split through committing some criminal act. Here crime is subject-conferring; it is a “mode of subjectivization.”

For Salecl, psychoanalysis is interested only in the crimes of the superego. For Mark Bracher, psychoanalysis is also concerned with crimes of the self, with various forms of narcissistic and alienating identifications. Aggression, for Bracher, cannot be reduced to purely psychological functioning. Bracher situates aggressivity and crime in the interplay of social and psychological forces. His is not a psychological reductionism, for he follows Lacan literally when the latter says that “neither crime nor criminals are objects that can be conceived outside of their sociological reference” (13). Lacan tells us that there does not exist a “criminal instinct” (24), for if there existed a “law of the jungle,” why are there not also “impulses to dig, to plant, to cook, and even to bury the dead”?

For both Salecl and Bracher, a certain amount of an excess in aggressivity finds its source in societal development, an insight generated by Freud in his Civilization and its Discontents. Salecl's exclusive emphasis on crime as a mode of subjectivization overlooks the insights of Freud, who implied that other outcomes are possible because of the dynamic of sublimation. “Inner tensions, inhibitions and traumas” (4) can find a means of expression, particularly in a mode of subjectivization by way of artistic and poetic expression, and other creative, and non-criminal outlets. Lacan's work on le sinthome, particularly in it application to the writings of James Joyce, suggests similar possibilities. Thus hope does exist, according to Bracher (following Lacan's account as opposed to Freud's), that excesses in both the quality and the quantity of aggressivity can be altered (5).

Tim Dean

Tim Dean

Tim Dean   Assistant Professor of English at the University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign, and this year is a Fellow at the Stanford Humanities Center, where he is working on a book to be titled “Modernism and the Ethics of Impersonality.” His Beyond the Couch: Sexuality, Psychoanalysis, and Cultural Politics is forthcoming.

In recent years it has become disturbingly apparent that safe-sex education programs need all the help they can get, simply because they aren't working effectively. After an initial decline in transmission rates during the eighties, the rate of infection has been climbing steadily in the very population group—urban gay men—that pioneered safe-sex education in the first place.1 With the advent of protease inhibitors (a class of new drugs that block an enzyme crucial to viral replication), AIDS may have become—for those lucky few who can afford and tolerate the drugs—a chronic rather than terminal condition, a manageable disease rather than a death sentence. And so as the interval lengthens between HIV infection and the likely onset of illness, gay men's principal deterrent for unprotected sex recedes, with potentially catastrophic implications. In this era of accelerating AIDS science and the resurgence of unsafe sexual practices, I'd like to explain how thinking psychoanalytically about the epidemic can help us grasp both the necessity for maintaining safe sex and some new strategies for doing so.

While it is notoriously difficult to generate accurate statistics about the rate of unsafe sex among gay men, the percentage one third has been repeated as axiomatic since the early 1990s—“one third of gay men are having buttsex without condoms” (Savage 11).2 What makes such estimates so striking is that even those who “know the facts” about HIV transmission continue to become infected with the virus that causes AIDS. Much of the evidence of escalating unsafe sex has been anecdotal, circulating privately, but also publicly in the form of third-person and, more remarkably, first-person accounts in the mainstream—as well as gay—media. When, in 1994, leading gay journalist Michelangelo Signorile and then, in 1995, prominent queer theorist Michael Warner both wrote about their own recent unsafe sexual encounters, these revelations highlighted the extent to which safe-sex education was failing. The problem penetrated mainstream national consciousness in 1996, thanks to a controversial New York Times Magazine cover story on Mark Ebenhoch, a thirtysomething, white gay man, who became HIV-positive for reasons other than simple lack of knowledge (see Green).3 Such high-profile accounts of individual cases dramatized what epidemiological data on seroconversion rates in the United States had been indicating since the early nineties—that basic information about AIDS, though indispensable, is nonetheless radically insufficient to stopping the epidemic.

William Ian Miller's latest book is not a psychoanalytic study of disgust. Although Miller is responsive to Freud's work, he tends to dismiss what he calls “depth psychology,” distancing his approach from psychoanalytic accounts of aversion, antipathy, and disgust. Such distancing is notable, and I'll comment on it here, but a review of Miller's book belongs in this journal because his interest in people's recoil from others—specifically, other people's bodies—has profound repercussions for a “psychoanalysis of culture and society.”

If we seek only to enhance our understanding of intimacy and group bonds, The Anatomy of Disgust will disappoint us. Discussing our recoil from such diverse phenomena as moldy food and used diapers, bad breath and earwax, Miller seems to be pushing chiefly for greater tolerance of the body's various secretions and smells. But The Anatomy of Disgust also reflects on our aversion to others' excessive proximity. Partly defeating the ameliorative aims of his prologue and opening chapter, Miller, in a later chapter on “Mutual Contempt and Democracy,” traces our structural inability to tolerate the most noxious aspects of living with other people.

Since Miller avows, in his preface, that his “general suspiciousness of and hostility to the reductionism of depth psychology threatened to obscure [his] better judgment” (xv), The Anatomy of Disgust avoids crudely assessing Freud's work. Miller's reading of Freud is generally fair, providing we pause when reading, “What is psychoanalysis, after all, but an attempt to make the journey inside us reduplicate the horrors and disgusts of an anthropological expedition into the heart of darkness?” (22).

That we seek to reduplicate various “horrors and disgusts” is a phenomenon worthy of study, signaling in part “the allure of the disgusting” (108), so it's a pity Miller does not clarify this “reduplication.” “There are ontological problems regarding the emotions,” he admits, “that I do not wish to discuss in detail” (9). Writing for a large audience (the New York Times Book Review and London Review of Books reviewed Anatomy, both raising doubts and reservations), Miller tends to downplay complex theoretical issues, but his discussion of Freud actually is the least psychoanalytic aspect of his book. Insights emerge elsewhere whose vigor and conceptual resonance take us far beyond his characterizations of “depth psychology.

The Context of the Conflict Resolution Process in Post-Soviet Estonia

The Center for the Study of Mind and Human Interaction (CSMHI) of the University of Virginia School of Medicine is an interdisciplinary center whose work in conflict resolution requires the collaboration of psychoanalysts, historians, diplomats and other scholars. Over the past decade, CSMHI has been invited to participate in the resolution of conflicts between nations as well as other related ethnonational and factional disputes. Following the breakup of the Soviet Union, Estonia wished to restore its political independence as well as its psychological independence. CSMHI had participated in other cases with participants from both Russia and Estonia and accordingly became an excellent credible candidate to assist both sides in the process of Estonia's psychopolitical independence from and co-existence with Russia as its neighbor. The methodology of CSMHI has been described elsewhere. One description of the methodology posits “four heuristic steps” (Apprey 199) in the conflict resolution process:

Intensive confidential interviews are conducted with a cross-section of leaders from all constituencies to ensure that CSMHI personnel understand the historical and contemporary concerns facing Estonians and Russians who have chosen to live in Estonia after the collapse of the Soviet Union.

A series of psychopolitical dialogues is initiated between representatives of interested parties (20-30 people in large, plenary sessions, to open and close each day of talks, and 8-10 people in small work group sessions). During this step, lines of communication are opened, concerns shared, and hidden psychological barriers that separate interested parties are brought to the surface, discussed, and ultimately transformed so that they no longer impede negotiation and movement toward common goals. The process often involves recognizing how historical relationships and events influence current relationships, how these relationships recur, and how they change function when they are perpetuated under different guises to serve new purposes. This second step is essential to the success of step three.

The last few years have witnessed an unprecedented succession of critical re-takes on Freudian fetishism across the fields of cultural studies, feminist theory, film studies, literary theory, queer theory, and visual culture. From within this gamut of critical re-readings, two tendencies have emerged. In broad terms, we can usefully differentiate historicizing re-contextualizing emphases, analyzing and describing fetishism's larger post-Enlightenment cultural stage, its cast of social and institutional actors, from rereadings of fetishism which analyze and expand interplays between the psychic and physical, fantasy and corporeality, desire and knowledge, subject and object in rethinking desire and sexuality. While overlaps and convergences abound, it is hardly surprising that the two tendencies articulate quite sharply distinct critical narratives about fetishism. While historicizing critics tend to resituate a still recognizable “Freud on fetishism”1 in broader and thicker (cultural, disciplinary, historical) contexts,2 that same “Freud on fetishism” becomes virtually unrecognizable, yet powerfully and resourcefully adaptable, in the work of contemporary feminisms and/or lesbian and gay studies. Here, by drawing on suggestive structural components, or contradictions, in Freud's text—particularly in the areas of disavowal, psychic investment in the material, and the fetishist's (pleasure in) ambivalence before the orthodox Freudian options—critics have read Freud against the grain. They have opened up critically transformative readings which account for non-heteronormative sexual desires, practices, and identifications otherwise illegible within—or abjected from—the available conception of desire, sexuality, and identity in psychoanalytic terms.3

Apter's Feminizing the Fetish not only imaginatively renegotiates elements of both tendencies of recent research, the historicizing and rearticulating of fetishism; she also enticingly, and energetically, extends the range and multiplies the contexts of nineteenth-century fetishism. Her bold, experimental scope, theoretical nimbleness, and scrupulously probing historical research emerge convincingly if we locate her project within, and yet also chronologically prior, to the expansion of research in these two directions.4 And yet, foregrounding, as we have done here, the tension, if not incompatibility, separating quite distinct roles accorded to fetishism within equally distinct critical objectives (to historicize, and rearticulate, fetishism), anticipates inevitable strains and stresses that the combinatory double move places on the project, which cause its overall surface coherence to buckle at times.

Rosaria Champagne

Rosaria Champagne   Assistant Professor of English at Syracuse University, where she teaches courses in queer theory, psychoanalysis, and feminism. She has published The Politics of Survivorship: Incest, Women's Literature, and Femninst Theory, and is currently working on a book on radical psychoanalysis and the Religious Right.

In June of 1996, a large, moneyed, and powerful emerging agent of the Religious Right, The Promise Keepers, held a revival meeting in Syracuse, NY, on the Syracuse University campus.2 Thirty-eight thousand and five hundred men, mostly white, mostly working class, dressed in dungarees and tee-shirts, slapping hands and yelling, “Score one for God!” arrived to spread the Word. The local newspaper, The Syracuse Post Standard, put out a special conference edition with the headline “WELCOME PROMISE KEEPERS!” Hotel rooms were booked from Rochester to Utica. The Carrier Dome, our lavish sports stadium, was transformed by huge TV screens. White tents covered the quad, set up to sell food and merchandise (PK sweatpants, PK tee shirts, PK water bottles, PK baseball caps, PK Day Planners, and mostly, PK books, all published by Focus on the Family). To the conservative Syracuse Common Council, The Promise Keepers were pennies from heaven. Syracuse University made a bundle, too. The Syracuse University administration requested that university workers depart early on the Friday of this flock's arrival, vacating needed parking spaces and giving our holy friends a wide berth. It cost each attendee $65.00. Women were not allowed. Some wives of the faithful facilitated the event as custodial workers or set up prayer circles on the campus lawn. There were no visible political protests.

It took me ten months to write about The Promise Keepers. Their invited presence in my community and university gave me—someone who rarely is at a loss of things to say—more than pause. It gave me near-paralysis. I have now responded to the Promise Keepers in two venues: a university lecture and an article in my local newspaper. Like most Academic Leftists, I have been trained to historicize oppressive institutions, and to recognize the importance of structural and economic forces that buttress ideologies, shape subjectivity, and limit agency. The Promise Keepers are ripe for such materialist investigations: with a $115 million projected annual operating budget, a staff of over 400 full-time employees, and additional sponsorship from Focus on the Family and The Christian Coalition, The Promise Keepers are hardly just a bad idea held by faith in the minds of a few devout Christian nationalists.3 In both my lecture to my colleagues and my article in the local paper, I labored to address my points with clarity, maintaining the myth that academics love to tell ourselves and others, the one that lets us get out of bed in the mornings: that knowledge produces social change. Indeed, I will argue here that “academic knowledge” (ideas that emerge within paradigms of interpretation and that are open to critique and change) can only function to produce action when recognized by the subject—and when subjects who hold competing “truths” recognize each other as subjects. Such recognition can be facilitated by an interpenetration of materialism with politicized psychoanalysis. Materialist analysis is necessary because producing epistemological “truths” is an important intellectual mandate: it provides the counter-discourse upon which subjectivites and social formations shift and develop. Psychoanalytic analysis is necessary because it offers a working knowledge of subjectivity that explains the limitations of materialism in two venues: the failure of materialism to inspire, and the arrogance of materialist theories in assuming that totalities are apprehendable outside of the (distortions of) the symbolic structure. The relationship between psychoanalytic and marxist-based materialist critique which I want to develop here can best be understood as a meaningful contradiction. I'm enthralled by the promise of materialism—you might even say I'm seduced by it.
